terms.definition: An S3 feature that prevents objects from being deleted or overwritten for a fixed retention period or indefinitely, enforcing WORM (Write Once, Read Many) storage.
terms.example: A financial firm enables Object Lock in Compliance Mode on audit logs to meet SEC 17a-4 regulations requiring 7-year immutable retention.

terms.definition: Write Once, Read Many — a storage model where data can be written once and read any number of times, but cannot be modified or deleted after the initial write.
terms.example: Compliance regulations like HIPAA and SEC often require WORM storage for sensitive records.

terms.definition: An Object Lock mode that protects objects from deletion by most users, but allows authorised users with special IAM permissions (like root) to overwrite objects.
terms.example: An internal development team uses Governance Mode to protect production code packages from accidental deletion while allowing release managers to update them.

terms.definition: An Object Lock mode that prevents all users — including root and AWS — from deleting or modifying an object during the retention period. The strictest Object Lock setting.
terms.example: Healthcare company uses Compliance Mode on patient records to satisfy HIPAA immutability requirements with no exceptions.

terms.definition: An Object Lock feature with no defined expiry date. The object remains locked until the legal hold is explicitly removed by an authorised user, regardless of any retention period.
terms.example: A corporation places a Legal Hold on email archives when a lawsuit is filed to preserve evidence indefinitely during litigation.

terms.definition: The process of converting readable data (plaintext) into unreadable data (ciphertext) using a cryptographic algorithm and key, so only authorised parties with the correct key can read it.
terms.example: S3 encrypts all stored objects so that even if physical storage media were stolen, the data would be unreadable without the encryption key.

terms.definition: An encryption approach where the same key is used for both encrypting and decrypting data. Faster than asymmetric encryption and used by S3 SSE-S3 (AES-256).
terms.example: SSE-S3 uses AES-256 symmetric encryption — the same key scrambles and unscrambles your S3 objects.

terms.definition: An encryption approach using a key pair: a public key for encryption and a private key for decryption. Used in SSL/TLS certificates for HTTPS.
terms.example: When your browser connects to https://example.com, it uses the website's public key to encrypt data that only the server's private key can decrypt.

terms.definition: Server-Side Encryption with S3 Managed Keys — the default S3 encryption where AWS automatically manages all encryption keys using AES-256, at no additional cost.
terms.example: Every new object uploaded to S3 is automatically protected with SSE-S3 with zero configuration required from the user.

terms.definition: Server-Side Encryption with AWS KMS keys — encryption where AWS Key Management Service manages the keys. Provides full audit trail via CloudTrail and allows fine-grained IAM-based key access control.
terms.example: A bank uses SSE-KMS for its transaction data bucket so every access attempt is logged in CloudTrail and only approved IAM roles can decrypt the data.

terms.definition: Server-Side Encryption with Customer Provided Keys — an S3 encryption option where the customer provides their own encryption key with each upload/download request. Being blocked from April 2026.
terms.example: A security-conscious company provides its own AES-256 key per API call for maximum key control — though this approach is being deprecated by AWS.

terms.definition: An encryption approach where the customer encrypts data on their own system before uploading to S3. S3 stores the pre-encrypted blob and never sees the plaintext data.
terms.example: A developer uses the AWS Encryption SDK to encrypt sensitive files on their laptop, then uploads the ciphertext to S3 — AWS never handles the plaintext.

terms.definition: AWS Key Management Service — a fully managed service for creating, storing, and controlling cryptographic keys used to encrypt data across AWS services.
terms.example: A cloud engineer uses KMS to create a Customer Managed Key for an S3 bucket, configure who can use it, and enable annual automatic rotation.

terms.definition: A KMS encryption key that you create and manage yourself in KMS — you control key policies, rotation, and access grants via IAM.
terms.example: A financial services team creates a CMK named 'transaction-data-key' and grants only the data-processing IAM role permission to use it for S3 encryption.

terms.definition: A KMS encryption key automatically created and managed by AWS on your behalf for use with specific AWS services. You cannot view, modify, or control its policies directly.
terms.example: When you first use SSE-KMS without specifying a key, AWS creates an AWS Managed Key named 'aws/s3' automatically in your account.

terms.definition: Hardware Security Module — a tamper-proof physical device that securely stores and processes cryptographic keys. KMS stores all master keys in HSMs to prevent extraction.
terms.example: Even AWS employees cannot extract a KMS master key from the HSM — the hardware physically destroys key material if tampering is detected.

terms.definition: Data Encryption Key — a temporary cryptographic key generated by KMS using your master key. S3 uses the DEK to actually encrypt individual objects, keeping the master key protected inside the HSM.
terms.example: When uploading a 5GB file to an SSE-KMS bucket, KMS generates a temporary DEK, S3 uses it to encrypt the file, then stores the encrypted DEK alongside the encrypted object.

terms.definition: An S3 cost optimisation feature that generates a single long-lived bucket-level DEK from one KMS call, then reuses it for many objects — reducing KMS API calls and charges by up to 99%.
terms.example: With 1 million daily uploads and Bucket Key enabled, S3 makes only one KMS call per bucket key refresh instead of 1 million separate KMS calls.

terms.definition: An S3 automation policy that moves objects to cheaper storage classes (transition action) or permanently deletes them (expiration action) based on the number of days since the object was created.
terms.example: A media company creates a lifecycle rule: transition raw video files to Glacier after 90 days and delete them after 3 years.

terms.definition: A lifecycle rule action that moves objects from one S3 storage class to another cheaper storage class after a specified number of days from the object's upload date.
terms.example: A transition action set to 30 days moves all objects from S3 Standard to S3 Standard-IA to reduce costs on data that is rarely accessed after the first month.

terms.definition: A lifecycle rule action that permanently deletes objects after a specified number of days from the upload date. Works with versioning to delete non-current versions and expired delete markers.
terms.example: A log management rule expires log files after 365 days to automatically clean up old data and avoid unbounded storage growth.

terms.definition: An S3 feature that automatically copies new objects from a source bucket to a destination bucket in a different AWS region for disaster recovery, compliance, or latency improvement.
terms.example: A Singapore-based company enables CRR from ap-southeast-1 to ap-south-1 so that Mumbai-region users can access content with lower latency.

terms.definition: An S3 feature that automatically copies new objects from a source bucket to a destination bucket within the same AWS region — for log aggregation, dev/prod sync, or internal backup.
terms.example: A DevOps team uses SRR to mirror the production log bucket into a centralised analytics bucket in the same region.

terms.definition: An S3 feature that serves HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and images directly from an S3 bucket over HTTP — without any web server — making it possible to host simple websites at near-zero cost.
terms.example: A developer hosts their personal portfolio at an S3 website endpoint, paying only a few cents per month for storage and data transfer.
